paras.text: The experiment was created using PsychoPy (Peirce et al., 2019) and was hosted on the Pavlovia platform (https://pavlovia.org). The experimental code was transformed into PsychoJS code. After giving informed consent via a mouse click, the narrative story embedding the S1R1 task was introduced: Participants were familiarised with instructions to take part in a magical tournament, called the “Trial of the Lions”, that involved passing a gate that was secured with two stone lions. The participants were informed that the lions would test their abilities in terms of speed, judgment, and depending on the group assignment, memory. Mirroring the procedure of an S1R1-S2R2 task, the lions would give them directional cues (R1 Cue) to test their speed (R1), show them the favourite fruits of the city’s royal couple (S2 and R2) to test the judgment abilities, and ask them questions about the order of presented fruits afterwards to test their memory in the memorizing group.

This experiment was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the German Association of Psychology (DGPs) and the Association of German Psychologists (BDP) and with the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki. The experiment was part of a research project which was approved by the University Research Ethics Committee of the University of Passau.3 In addition, the experiment was pre-registered at aspredicted.org (#190,425, https://aspredicted.org/dgbc-cmx3.pdf).

Sample size was estimated via power contours (Baker et al., 2021) using pilot data from two independent studies on the same topic (within SD = 161.00 ms, between SD = 133.04 ms and mean difference in PRCs, which represent the S-R interaction, PRC difference = 76.40 ms). Compared to traditional power analysis methods, which focus solely on sample size and do not consider the number of trials per participant, power contours simultaneously optimize both the number of participants and the number of trials per participant, with the relative magnitude of within- versus between-participant variance determining what the critical trial number is for achieving adequate power. For desired power of 95% and 32 trials per Response Stimulus Interval (RSI) factor level, data had to be collected from 210 participants. Although this resulted in only four trials per condition, power was ensured by recruiting a large sample consistent with the recommendation that power can be improved by increasing either the number of trials or the number of participants (Miller, 2024). A total of 232 participants were recruited via an online panel service (Bilendi, https://www.bilendi.de/) (116 participants per group). Seven participants were excluded due to excessive error rates in the first response (R1, 3 participants) or the second response (R2, 4 participants) amounting to at least 40% overall error rates in R1 or R2 (given a valid R1 response) (as compared with an average of 8.27% in R1 and 6.73% in R2), suggesting either their inability or unwillingness to follow the instruction. Additionally, one participant was excluded due to a lack of correct responses in one condition.4 Finally, one participant was excluded due to excessive time to complete the experiment (323 minutes compared to average of 20 minutes).5 No one was excluded due to excessive error rate in memory checks for S1 within the memorizing group (M = 5.14%, SD = 5.22%). In the final sample, 109 participants remained in the memorizing group and 114 in the control group, respectively. The total sample of N = 223 (176 women, 46 men, 1 diverse), ranged in age from 18 to 30 years (M = 24.63, SD = 3.18).

Features such as the person’s face (stimulus) and the spoken name (response) and their link are retained together and are assumed to be bound into a common episodic representation unit,1 often called an event file or a stimulus-response (S-R) episode (for overviews, see Hommel, 2004, and Binding and Retrieval Framework, BRAC, Frings et al., 2020). When any feature of an event file is re-encountered, the entire event file is assumed to be retrieved. Such retrieval can impair performance if the retrieved information partially mismatches either the subsequent stimulus or response. S–R binding and retrieval is typically measured using sequential paradigms, in which binding takes place in a so-called prime and event-file retrieval is assessed in a subsequent probe (Frings et al., 2020).

One well-established example of a sequential prime-probe presentation task is the S1R1-S2R2 paradigm (Hommel, 1998, 2005). In this paradigm, each trial typically begins with a cue (R1 cue) indicating the first response to be performed (R1). An initial stimulus (S1) is then presented, and participants execute R1 as instructed by the cue. Next, a second stimulus (S2) appears, requiring a second response (R2) according to a probe-response rule that remains constant throughout the experiment. Partial or complete feature overlap between S1/R1 and S2/R2 systematically influences R2 performance: repeating only stimulus- or response-related features between successive trials leads to longer response times and/or increased error rates as compared with full or no repetitions, also termed partial repetition costs (PRCs, Hommel, 2004).

Hommel’s theory of event coding characterizes event files as transient bindings that can be automatically retrieved, but it does not specify an explicit mechanism for sustained, attention-based maintenance in working memory or short-term memory (Hommel, 1998, 2004, 2009). In the BRAC framework (Frings et al., 2020) event files are conceptualized as memory-like entries comparable to Logan’s instances (Logan, 1988). More recent accounts propose that initial bindings vary in entry strength, partly depending on the activation of stimulus and response features through repetition and the time between repetitions. Only bindings that reach a certain strength threshold are assumed to be encoded in long-term memory; weaker bindings remain transient in short-term memory (Frings et al., 2024). Other accounts propose that event files are actively maintained in working memory via object-based attention, allowing recently integrated stimulus and response features to remain accessible (Lu et al., 2019). At present, it remains unclear how memory contributes to the formation and use of event files, and whether S–R bindings are solely short-lived, transient representations (Frings et al., 2024; Frings et al., 2020; Hommel, 1998), or can also become longer-lasting bindings. However, consensus is that memory plays a central role in S–R binding and retrieval. Yet, despite being recognized as a core aspect of event file research, direct empirical evidence on how memory shapes binding and retrieval and the lifespan of event files remains sparse.

Regarding the lifespan of event files, increasing the interval between event-file formation and later retrieval tends to reduce the impact of previous event files on performance, suggesting that event files are retrieved less strongly (or less frequently) over time (Frings et al., 2022; Hommel & Frings, 2020). In line with this, two studies varying several intervals between prime and probe trials have confirmed smaller PRCs with increasing intervals (Hommel & Frings, 2020). These results have been interpreted as evidence for decay rather than interference as the source of this decline: Hommel and Frings (2020) found no systematic effect of intervening stimuli or stimulus-response events on the drop in PRCs over time, and concluded that the reduction reflects the passage of time itself. It is worth noting that this decay is generally understood as a fading of activation in the bound codes rather than a dissolution of the link between them (Hommel & Colzato, 2004). In this view, an event file that has decayed may still be structurally intact, but harder to retrieve, rather than gone entirely.

This decay is not uniform across all binding types, however. How long a binding survives appears to depend on whether the bound feature was task-relevant. Frings (2011) and Frings et al. (2017) found that distractor-response bindings, formed from task-irrelevant features, survived a 500 ms interval but were no longer detectable after 2000 ms, whereas bindings involving task-relevant (target) features tend to persist over considerably longer intervals (Frings et al., 2022). Frings et al. (2022) directly compared target and distractor bindings within the same task and found that although target bindings were more durable overall, the two decayed at a comparable rate, differing mainly in their initial binding strength rather than in how quickly that strength was lost.

Based on this body of research, it has been discussed that the lifespan of event files is determined by attention, by shaping entry binding strength via attention allocation to relevant features and/or their attentional weighting in the binding process (Frings et al., 2020; Hommel, 2004). Hommel and Colzato (2004) investigated the effect of attention on the time course of event files and found that event files were more persistent across stimulus-onset asynchronies (SOAs) when the features of the first presented stimulus were attended than when they were unattended. In their second experiment, a visual version of the S1R1-S2R2 task (Hommel, 1998, 2005) was employed. The S1 and S2 were separated by an SOA ranging from 1,100 ms to 4,100 ms. In half of the six sessions, participants were instructed to pay attention to the S1—in other words, to memorize the features of the S1—as they had to respond to questions about one (of three) random S1 features after the trial. PRCs were largest at the shortest SOA and then decreased with increasing SOA levels in both response times and error rates, though they remained reliable even at the longest SOA. The effects of SOA on the PRCs were further modulated by the attention manipulation, but only in error rates, with event files being more persistent across SOAs when the S1 features were attended than when they were unattended. However, the authors concluded that attention was not necessary to observe the effect, and that the effect of attention and time on event files is rather limited, because PRCs were still present at the longest SOA in error rates.

Despite this progress, evidence for a mechanism affecting the event file longevity remains inconclusive, partly because previous studies focused on inducing decay to diminish memory traces (e.g. by added interfering stimuli or increasing intervals between presentations) or on attention processes that determine entry binding strength. Comparatively little consideration was given to factors that may support the persistence of event files once formed. In paradigms studying binding and retrieval, participants are typically not explicitly instructed to remember or memorize specific features (except see Hommel & Colzato, 2004).

Yet, processes such as rehearsal or attentional refreshing can preserve information in memory and counteract the loss of activation over time (Glavan & Houpt, 2019; Ricker et al., 2016). While both attentional refreshing and articulatory rehearsal can counteract memory loss, they operate via distinct mechanisms: attentional refreshing reactivates memory traces by directing attention toward them, whereas articulatory rehearsal maintains information through subvocal repetition via the phonological loop (Glavan & Houpt, 2019). Assuming that an event file is stored in short-term memory2 (Frings et al., 2024), manipulations designed to enhance short-term memory should prolong the persistence of these representations, leading to longer-lasting binding effects, operationalized here as larger PRCs. The present study aimed to test this possibility to clarify whether and how these memory processes affect event-file decay.

Following the idea that event files constitute short-term memory representations, manipulations that affect memory should influence the time course of transient event files. In this study, we incorporated elements from the narrative paradigm (Ezzyat & Davachi, 2011; Speer & Zacks, 2005) in a verbal version of the well-established S1R1-S2R2 task (Hommel, 1998) to increase the richness and concreteness of episodic representations. Robust binding and retrieval effects have been found with this task version in a previous study (Scotts et al., 2026).

We aimed to investigate whether instructing participants to memorize to later report the identity of an event-file element (S1) can affect PRCs. Beside the manipulation of the interval between event file formation (prime) and retrieval (probe), we manipulated whether participants were instructed to memorize information from the prime. Specifically, in the so-called memorizing condition, participants were asked to report the identity of the first stimulus (S1) after each trial. This requirement should promote rehearsal or attentional refreshing, which may counteract decay and help preserve information in memory (Glavan & Houpt, 2019; Ricker et al., 2016). Given that the stimuli in the present study were verbal, phonological rehearsal may be the more likely candidate mechanism underlying any memory benefit in the memorizing group.

PRCs were expected to be smaller following long R1-S2 intervals (i.e. 5,000 milliseconds) than short R1-S2 intervals (i.e. 500 milliseconds). In contrast to related work that manipulated S1-S2 SOAs (Hommel & Colzato, 2004; Hommel & Frings, 2020), we manipulated response-stimulus intervals (RSIs) between R1 and S2 to investigate event-file decay. RSIs appeared to be the most direct and cleanest implementation of a retention interval as it has been argued that the R1 response completes event-file formation and effectively closes the event file (Frings et al., 2020; Hommel, 2004). SOAs between S1 and S2, in contrast, conflate inter- and intra-individually varying R1 reaction time latencies and the actual retention interval. Consequently, RSIs may provide more direct control over the temporal distance between event file formation and retrieval than SOAs.

This experiment was part of a larger series of experiments in which we incorporated elements from the narrative paradigm (Ezzyat & Davachi, 2011; Speer & Zacks, 2005) in the well-established S1R1-S2R2 task (Hommel, 1998). Specifically, narrative texts were embedded in the task to create an impression of a story-telling role-play game. Each trial started with the presentation of a textual response cue (R1 Cue) followed by a prime (S1R1) and a probe (S2R2) presentation: For the R1 Cue, the German words for “Die Löwen: Rechts” or “Die Löwen: Links” (meaning “The lions: right” or “The lions: left” respectively) were presented for 2,000 ms, indicating a left or right response (R1) to perform at the time of the first stimulus (S1). The S1 was presented for up to 1,000 ms or until the R1 was performed. Although the S1 sentences varied (either the German words “Eine Birne erscheint” or “Eine Orange erscheint” meaning “A pear appears” or “An orange appears”, respectively), participants were instructed to respond solely with the response signalled by the cue, regardless of the identity of the S1. The relationship between the sentence presented as S1 and the response required in R1 was completely arbitrary. Responses were made using two spatially compatible keys (“f” for left and “j” for right) on a keyboard. Participants used the index fingers of each hand to press the keys.

Response times and error rates of R2 (given a correct R1) were of primary interest. The experiment comprises a 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 mixed design with RSI (500 ms vs. 5,000 ms), Stimulus (S1-S2, repeated vs. changed) and Response (R1-R2, repeated vs. changed) as within-subject variables and Memorization (memorizing vs. control) as between-subject variable, leading to 16 experimental conditions. Binding and retrieval effects are signified by the interaction between stimulus and response features, reflecting the integration and retrieval of event files. Partial repetition costs (reflecting the stimulus response interaction) for response times and error rates were calculated from the participants means in each condition as follows: (StimulusChanged ResponseRepeated – StimulusRepeated ResponseRepeated) – (Stimulus Changed ResponseChanged – StimulusRepeated ResponseChanged) (e.g., Stoet & Hommel, 1999).

In this experiment, we investigated whether the instruction to memorize the identity of an event-file element (S1) affects the persistence of event files, indexed by PRCs. Assuming that event files are stored in short-term memory, maintaining the memory trace of an event file should influence its life span. In other words, we proposed a memory trace will last longer in the memorizing group as compared with the control group. Based on previous work (Hommel & Frings, 2020), we assumed smaller PRCs after long as compared with short prime-probe RSI. Additionally, we expected larger PRCs for the memorizing group as compared with the control group after the long RSI, whereas we expected no difference or a smaller difference between the two groups after the short RSI.

As predicted and in line with previous work (Hommel & Frings, 2020), overall PRCs were smaller after long (i.e. 5,000 ms) as compared with short (i.e., 500 ms) R1-S2 RSIs in response times and error rates, indicating that retrieval of event files is reduced after long RSIs. Previously, this reduction in PRCs over longer intervals has been attributed to decay (Hommel & Frings, 2020), consistent with an account in which the link between bound codes persists but becomes harder to reactivate over time. Furthermore, PRCs in response times and error rates in our study were also generally larger when S1 had to be explicitly memorized compared to when no instruction was given to memorize it. In response times, this effect of Memorization was not modulated by time (RSI): the instruction to memorize improved the retrieval of event files at all levels of the RSI factor. In error rates, PRCs differed between the groups after short RSIs but not after long RSIs.

This dissociation between response times and error rates is worth being addressed. In response times, the memorizing group showed larger PRCs than the control group at both RSIs equally; in error rates, this group difference was present at the short RSI but not the long RSI. This is not a classic speed-accuracy trade-off, which would predict opposite directions across the two measures. A more likely explanation is that the two measures differ in their sensitivity. Measure-specific sensitivity has also been reported in other event-file literature: Hommel and Colzato (2004) reported several effects, including the impact of stimulus location repetition, that were significant in one measure but not the other, and interpreted this as reflecting differences in how sensitive each measure is to the underlying process rather than evidence for two dissociable effects. The same explanation likely applies here, though we cannot rule out that the RT effect is present but underpowered to detect the interaction specifically, given that the main effect of Memorization in response times was reliable.

We attribute this shift toward non-significance in the error-rate interaction to reduced power rather than to a disappearance of the underlying effect. This does not undermine the broader pattern: the overall tendency toward larger PRCs in the memorizing group held across both response times and error rates, and across the full and restricted samples alike. Rather than slowing the decay of an existing memory trace, the instruction to memorize may instead have strengthened the initial binding of stimulus and response features. This interpretation is consistent with recent accounts proposing that entry binding strength determines the retrievability of event files over time, such that stronger bindings are retrieved more reliably regardless of the elapsed interval (Frings et al., 2024). Attention allocated to stimulus features during encoding is one factor proposed to increase entry binding strength (Frings et al., 2024), and the requirement to memorize the S1 identity may have directed attention toward the S1 in a way that enhanced this initial binding in addition to supporting active maintenance over the delay.

Hommel and Colzato (2004) argued that binding does not depend on attention or available attentional resources per se, but is instead governed by the current task goal: once a goal makes a particular feature dimension relevant, that relevance can be held in working memory and lend top-down support to the corresponding feature, after which integration proceeds automatically without further effort. Our memorization instruction can be understood as one way of establishing such a task goal, making S1 identity relevant in a way it was not for the control group, which is consistent with Hommel’s and Colzato’s account. Relatedly, event files were more persistent across SOAs when attention was directed to S1 features, in error rates, in Hommel and Colzato’s (2004) own data. However, Hommel’s and Colzato’s conclusion concerned whether attention is necessary for binding to occur, whereas our findings speak to whether a memorization instruction can enhance the persistence of an already-formed event file. These are compatible claims: our control group, which showed reliable PRCs without any memorization instruction, replicated Hommel’s and Colzato’s finding that binding does not require attention. The data from the memorizing group showed, in addition, that explicitly instructing participants to retain S1 can strengthen this effect further.

When comparing the two studies, several further differences should be noted. In the present study, only a single verbal stimulus (i.e. identity of the object) had to be memorized instead of three features (colour, shape, location) in the study of Hommel and Colzato (2004). Using a single stimulus feature likely facilitated phonological rehearsal and may have strengthened the influence of memory on event-file representations. With respect to the interval type, the temporal distance between S1 and S2 is shorter when SOAs are used, as in Hommel and Colzato (2004), than when the same intervals are employed as RSIs, as in the present study, because the participants’ response time is added to the interval in the latter case. Longer intervals may increase the risk of attenuating binding and retrieval effects (Hommel & Colzato, 2004; Hommel & Frings, 2020). Nevertheless, partial repetition costs, the index of binding and retrieval effects, were observed even following the long RSIs (5,000 ms) in our study, despite the longer elapsed time between S1 and S2 (up to 6,000 ms) compared to long SOAs (4,000 ms) in Hommel and Colzato (2004), as in absolute terms, the type of interval (RSI vs. SOA) does make a difference for the time elapsed between S1 and S2. By controlling the interval between response and subsequent stimulus, rather than between stimuli, the interval manipulation targets stimulus–response integration more directly and is in line with the common assumption that the response completes and effectively closes an event file (Frings et al., 2020; Hommel, 2004). This indicates that using RSIs instead of SOAs does not compromise and may even strengthen the experimental design and event-file formation. Finally, with N = 223, the present study is considerably larger than Hommel and Colzato (2004), N = 16, providing substantially greater statistical power to detect modulations of attention on the time course of PRCs, keeping in mind that between-subject designs are statistically less sensitive than within-subject designs.
Yet, there is an ongoing discussion of how the stimulus and response features are precisely retained. Another view suggests that features and their links are stored separately (Verwey, 2024).
